id: Love Poem So Tall It Ends in Heaven

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A man I loved kept a folded square of masking tape in his pocket He did this / only for a year His masking tape was bright orange and fraying As evidence / coroners had used it to attach to his father’s calf the rope his father’d used / This man planted the tape in our yard when the year was done and from it grew thirteen beams / From these beams rafters grew Ropes uncurled from these rafters and fathers hanged from the ropes / Over the fathers a roof blossomed like a shield and against it a ladder leaned / The ladder was so tall the man I loved said it must have ended in heaven And down / from the ladder an angel scurried while we slept In its mouth it carried torn strips / of tape The angel pressed this tape on the calves of the man I loved like bandages / Each morning I removed the tape I was careful not to wake him Each morning / he’d walk through the garden of swaying fathers He’d kneel beside our rosemary bush / He’d rub its leaves in his hands He’d ball his hands in his hair to scent it He wanted / just to keep his earthliness with him / In hell this is the only prerequisite

The text explores inherited grief, suicide, and the burden of traumatic evidence through surreal imagery in which a keepsake of masking tape grows into a house-like structure filled with hanging fathers and angelic attempts at repair. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: His, This, From

outputs.L1:
A man I loved kept a folded square of masking tape in his pocket. He did this only for a year. His masking tape was bright orange and fraying. As evidence, coroners had used it to attach to his father’s calf the rope his father had used.

When the year was done, this man planted the tape in our yard, and from it grew thirteen beams. From these beams, rafters grew. Ropes uncurled from the rafters, and fathers hanged from the ropes. Over the fathers, a roof blossomed like a shield, and against it leaned a ladder.

The ladder was so tall that the man I loved said it must have ended in heaven. And down from the ladder, while we slept, an angel scurried. In its mouth, it carried torn strips of tape. The angel pressed this tape to the calves of the man I loved like bandages.

Each morning, I removed the tape. I was careful not to wake him. Each morning, he walked through the garden of swaying fathers. He knelt beside our rosemary bush. He rubbed its leaves in his hands. He balled his hands in his hair to scent it. He wanted only to keep his earthliness with him.

In hell, this is the only prerequisite.
outputs.L2:
A man I once loved carried, tucked in his pocket, a small folded piece of masking tape. He did this for exactly one year. The tape was vivid orange and worn at the edges. It had been used as evidence: the coroners had fastened, to his father’s calf, the rope his father had used.

When the year ended, the man I loved buried the tape in our yard. From that spot, thirteen beams rose. Rafters emerged from the beams. Ropes loosened and dropped from the rafters, and fathers hung from those ropes. Above the fathers, a roof opened out like a protective shield, and a ladder rested against it.

The ladder reached so high that the man I loved said it must have led all the way to heaven. While we slept, an angel hurried down from it, carrying shredded pieces of tape in its mouth. The angel placed the tape on the calves of the man I loved, as if dressing wounds.

Every morning, I peeled the tape away, taking care not to wake him. Every morning, he moved through the garden where the fathers swayed. He knelt near our rosemary bush, crushed its leaves between his palms, then pressed his hands into his hair so the scent would stay there. He wanted only to carry some trace of earth with him.

In hell, that is the single requirement.
outputs.L3:
A man carried, folded in his pocket, a fraying square of bright orange masking tape. Its color had once been vivid enough to stop the eye, the kind of orange used to warn, to mark, to say do not cross. Now it was dulled by lint, sweat, and the constant rubbing of his thumb. The tape had been removed from the room where his father died and sealed for a time in a plastic evidence bag, labeled in black ink, numbered, handled by strangers. Later, when the investigation was finished and there was nothing left to prove, it was returned with the other belongings. The man kept it because it had touched the last arrangement of his father’s life. He carried it the way some people carry a coin, a prayer card, or a stone from a grave.

For a year he did not know what to do with it. He took it out at bus stops, in grocery lines, at his kitchen table in the hour before dawn. He unfolded it and folded it again, though the corners had begun to split and the adhesive had long ago given up its purpose. Sometimes he imagined throwing it away. Sometimes he imagined framing it. Mostly he let it remain close to his body, warmed by him, as if warmth could change what had happened or soften the image it preserved.

At the end of that year, on an evening that smelled of damp soil and cut grass, the man went into the yard and dug a narrow hole with a garden trowel. He laid the orange square inside as carefully as if he were planting a bulb. He covered it with earth, pressed the soil flat with both hands, and stood over it until darkness erased the outline of the spot.

By morning, the yard had changed.

From the place where he had buried the tape, pale wooden beams had risen. Rafters angled into the air, raw and unfinished, forming the skeleton of a house that had no walls. Ropes hung from the crosspieces in terrible loops, and from those ropes hung fathers—not one father, but many. They swayed slightly in the early wind, their faces shadowed, their shoes motionless above the grass. Some looked like his father. Some looked like fathers he had never known. Some seemed only like the idea of fatherhood made heavy and suspended: silence, authority, absence, grief.

The man did not scream. He stood in his garden with his hands at his sides, understanding that what he had planted had taken root according to its own nature. Evidence had become architecture. Memory had become a structure he could walk beneath.

Then, as the day brightened, another change appeared. Above the hanging fathers, a roof formed—first a shimmer, then shingles, then a broad protective covering that shielded them from rain and sun. It did not excuse the scene beneath it, nor did it conceal it, but it made a kind of shelter over the unbearable. Beside the beams, a ladder appeared, reaching upward farther than the man could see. Its rungs were narrow and silvered with light. He thought of it as a ladder to heaven, though he did not know whether heaven was a destination, a release, or simply the word people used for a place beyond explanation.

After that, the garden became part of his life. He did not remove the beams. He did not cut the ropes. He did not climb the ladder. He learned instead to pass through the yard carefully, as one moves through a room where someone is sleeping or dying. The fathers swayed above him in all seasons. In rain, the roof held. In winter, frost silvered the ropes. In spring, weeds grew around the posts, and bees moved among the clover below their dangling feet.

Each night, an angel descended.

It came quietly, after the last lights in the neighborhood went out. The man would wake to the sensation of cool air entering the room and find the angel kneeling beside his bed. It carried strips of bright orange tape, fresh and luminous, as if torn from an endless roll kept somewhere beyond the visible world. Without speaking, the angel placed the strips across the man’s calves. It laid them there like bandages, smoothing them over the muscle and bone with hands that were neither warm nor cold. The tape did not hurt when it touched him. It did not heal him in any simple way. But it held something together during the hours when sleep made him defenseless.

By morning, the strips were always gone. No residue remained on his skin, no proof except for a faint tenderness in his legs and the memory of being tended to by something that did not ask him to explain his sorrow.

Each morning, the man rose and went into the haunting garden. He passed beneath the rafters and the ropes, beneath the fathers who were his and not his, beneath the roof that protected even what was painful to behold. He would pause at the foot of the ladder and look up until his neck ached, but he never climbed. Not yet.

Before leaving the yard, he bent to the rosemary bush growing near the back steps. He crushed a few needles between his fingers and rubbed the scent onto his wrists, his throat, and the backs of his hands. The fragrance was sharp, green, and earthly. It reminded him of kitchens, rain, lamb roasting in ovens, old women’s gardens, and the stubborn life of plants that survive poor soil. He scented himself with rosemary so he would not drift too far into the world of beams and ropes, angels and fathers, evidence and heaven. He did it to preserve his sense of earthliness.

Then he went on with the day, carrying the smell of rosemary with him, while behind him the garden waited—sheltered, terrible, and alive.
outputs.L4:
The text explores the way grief can be inherited, preserved, and physically carried long after the original wound has occurred. At its center is a keepsake made of masking tape, an ordinary and fragile object that becomes charged with unbearable meaning. What begins as a small remnant of memory grows, through surreal and dreamlike imagery, into something much larger: a house-like structure, a place the speaker can enter but not escape. This house is not a shelter in any comforting sense. Instead, it is a chamber of traumatic evidence, filled with fathers who hang like repeated signs of loss, absence, and self-destruction.

The image of the “hanging fathers” suggests that suicide is not presented as a single isolated event, but as something that echoes through generations. The dead are suspended in memory, never fully gone and never fully at rest. Their presence turns grief into an architecture: the mourner lives inside what has happened. The masking tape, a material associated with temporary repair, holding things together, or marking off damage, becomes an inadequate but powerful symbol. It cannot truly mend the rupture, yet it preserves the shape of it. It holds the evidence in place.

Against this devastation, the text introduces angelic figures or gestures of repair. These angels seem to represent the desire to heal, to rescue, or to make the broken world whole again. Yet their efforts are limited. They may tend to the wound, cover it, or hover near it, but they cannot undo the death or erase its consequences. Their presence emphasizes both compassion and helplessness. Even what is sacred or merciful cannot fully release the mourner from the burden of knowing.

The text therefore suggests that mourning is not something that can be completed neatly. It cannot be cured by explanation, ritual, memory, or even love. Grief remains, changing shape but not disappearing. The mourner may try to transform it into an object, a house, a story, or a vision, but each transformation reveals how deeply the loss has entered the imagination. The traumatic evidence persists because it belongs not only to the past, but also to the body and senses of the living.

Yet the text does not end in total abstraction or despair. It turns toward ordinary sensory life, especially the scent of rosemary, as a fragile but necessary anchor. Rosemary, with its associations of remembrance, earth, food, and touch, offers a connection to the living world. It keeps the beloved man from becoming only a symbol of death or grief. Through such a simple scent, he remains human: someone who breathed, touched, loved, and belonged to the everyday world.

In this way, the text balances surreal horror with tenderness. It recognizes that the dead cannot be restored and that mourning cannot be fully escaped. But it also insists that memory does not have to belong only to trauma. The beloved can be held not only through the terrible evidence of his death, but through the small, fragrant details of life. The scent of rosemary becomes a modest form of resistance, keeping him tethered to humanity when grief threatens to turn him into nothing more than an emblem of loss.
outputs.L5: His journey began with a simple idea. This idea grew into something meaningful because it came from determination, patience, and hard work. From every challenge, he learned a lesson, and from every success, he found new motivation. This shows that progress often starts with small steps, but with focus and courage, it can lead to great achievements.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about grief after a father’s suicide, using the recurring image of orange masking tape, with slashes for line breaks and a dark mythic ending.
counterfactuals.output:
After my father died by his own hand, the house began labeling itself / orange masking tape on the mirror, orange masking tape on the bread, orange masking tape across the mouth of the clock / as if time were evidence / as if grief needed a border to keep from flooding the cabinets /

I found strips of it in places he had never touched / wound around the stems of dead tulips / pasted over the eyes in family photographs / sealing shut the little cardboard box where he kept screws, washers, keys to nothing / each piece bright as a warning flare / each piece saying: not here, not anymore, not your father /

At night the tape unspooled from the walls like a tongue / licked the floorboards / measured the hallway from my bedroom to the locked door of his absence / I followed it barefoot through rooms that bent like wet paper / past the kitchen where the kettle whistled in his voice / past the chair that sat with its back turned / past the window where the moon hung, bruised and citrus-colored, wrapped in orange masking tape /

In dreams he returned as a stag with a human shadow / antlers tangled in extension cords / throat full of moths / he knelt in the yard and let me peel tape from his ribs, strip by strip / beneath it there was no wound / only more tape / bright and endless / the color of traffic cones, hospital bracelets, the last light before a tunnel closes /

I wanted to ask why / but the question had been taped shut / I wanted to be angry / but anger wore his jacket and would not look at me / I wanted to forgive him / but forgiveness was a room with no furniture, no door, and the orange tape running ceiling to floor like a vein /

So I carried the roll into the woods / where the old stories still breathe under stones / I marked the trees one by one / father, father, father / until the forest became a corridor of small suns / until the path behind me vanished / until the black river opened its mouth /

There, on the bank, the dead were waiting / faceless, patient, crowned with roots / and among them stood my father, holding the loose end of the tape / he did not speak / he only pulled /

The orange line tightened between us / a leash, a lifeline, a fuse / and from beneath the river rose the ancient god of endings / antlers of bone, eyes like extinguished lamps / he wrapped the tape around my father’s wrists, then mine / binding us not together, but to the dark /

Then he struck a match against the moon / and the tape began to burn without flame / glowing orange in the underworld wind / leading my father down / leading me back / leaving the trees marked, the river hungry, and the night sealed shut behind him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary lyric poem in one paragraph about a lover who carries evidence from his father’s death, plants it, and grows a haunted house full of fathers, angels, ropes, and rosemary.
counterfactuals.output: My lover keeps the evidence in a blue envelope under the bed: ash, a button, the hospital bracelet cut clean as a throat, the last voicemail buzzing like a wasp in its little plastic hive. At dusk he goes into the yard and plants each piece with his bare hands, pressing the dirt down gently, as if tucking in a child or a verdict. All night the ground knocks back. By morning a house has risen there, black-roofed and breathing, its windows wet with recognition, its porch swing moving though no one has touched it. Inside, every room is full of fathers—fathers in work boots, fathers in Sunday shirts, fathers asleep in recliners with their mouths open to the weather, fathers calling from behind walls, fathers who do not know they are dead and keep asking for the light. Angels crowd the stairwell like tenants, shedding feathers into the vents, their faces bright and useless as coins. Ropes bloom from the ceilings, soft as vines, tying the rafters to the wrists of memory. Rosemary grows through the floorboards, bitter and green, perfuming the kitchen where no meal is ever finished. My lover walks room to room with soil under his nails, listening for the one voice that made him, the one silence that unmade him, while the house leans closer, father after father opening their arms, saying son, saying stay, saying look what grief can build when you bury it alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an unsettling, dreamlike poem in the style of modern confessional surrealism, centered on inherited trauma, suicide, and a man trying to remain earthly.
counterfactuals.output:
My father left me a room inside his ribs,  
wallpapered in weather reports and unpaid light.  
At night I go there barefoot,  
trying not to wake the old furniture—  
the chair that knows the rope,  
the mirror that keeps practicing absence.

There is a country my family never names.  
Its border is a kitchen table.  
Its flag is a towel darkening under the faucet.  
Everyone I love has citizenship  
in some emergency of the blood.

I was born after the worst thing happened,  
which means the worst thing happened  
again, in miniature,  
inside my mouth before language.

Mother says: eat.  
The dead say: echo.  
The house says: choose a window  
and become weather.

But I am trying to remain earthly.

I press my palms to dirt  
as if apologizing to a large animal.  
I learn the ordinary sacraments:  
soup, shoelace, rent,  
the rude green insistence of onions.  
I let the dog pull me down the block  
past hedges glittering with sprinkler light,  
past children shrieking like souls  
that have not yet been assigned a history.

Still, some mornings  
the ceiling lowers its gray face  
and whispers my family name.  
Still, the bathtub fills with snow.  
Still, my wrists remember  
stories they were never told.

I have inherited a locked drawer  
and the key is made of my own pulse.  
Inside: a photograph of a man  
standing too close to the edge of himself,  
his smile a match struck in rain.  
I want to call him back  
from whatever black orchard received him.  
I want to say: stay,  
there is coffee going cold on the counter,  
there is a sparrow dismantling the dawn,  
there is still a body here, stubborn and warm,  
wearing your sorrow like a second coat.

But the dead do not come back.  
They send weather.  
They send dreams where the hallway lengthens  
and every door opens onto the same small room  
where someone has just left  
and the lamp is still swinging.

So I plant my feet.  
I name each thing that will have me:  
floorboard, bread, blue cup,  
moth in the sink like a fallen thought.  
I carry my grief carefully,  
not as a weapon, not as a child,  
but as a glass of water through a burning house.

If I spill, I begin again.

The earth does not forgive me.  
It does not need to.  
It offers mud, gravity,  
the blunt sermon of stones.  
It says: remain.  
It says: bruise, then berry.  
It says: even the root, buried alive,  
keeps reaching.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose-poem with no stanza breaks about a man I loved, a folded square of masking tape, coroners, a ladder to heaven, an angel applying bandages at night, and the line “In hell this is the only prerequisite.”
counterfactuals.output: The man I loved kept a folded square of masking tape in his wallet as if it were a photograph, as if adhesive could remember what skin forgets, and when he opened it the corners lifted like little wings tired of being told they were only paper. He said everything worth saving needed a temporary repair: a cracked taillight, a child’s cardboard crown, the mouth of an envelope, the heart when it began making that soft animal noise in the dark. After he died, the coroners moved around him with the careful boredom of priests after a festival, naming the body by its failures, weighing the silence, writing down the weather in his blood. I wanted to ask them if love ever showed up under the ribs, if grief had a measurable temperature, if they had seen, tucked beneath his tongue, the small ladder to heaven he had been building all his life out of apologies and matchsticks and the names of everyone he could not bear to leave. At night I still hear him climbing: one rung creaks like our kitchen chair, another like the hinge of the medicine cabinet, another like my voice when I said stay and meant forgive me. Sometimes an angel comes in through the window with her sleeves rolled up, smelling faintly of rain and iodine, and applies bandages to the places where memory keeps reopening me; she tapes gauze across my dreams, presses two fingers to my wrist, and tells me not to mistake the wound for the door. But I have seen the door. It is small and yellowed and stuck to itself. It is the folded square of masking tape, carried close to the body until even the glue learns devotion. In hell this is the only prerequisite. To have loved something mortal enough to try to mend it, again and again, with whatever poor materials the world allowed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark magical-realist poem where a piece of evidence from a death is buried in a yard and grows into beams, rafters, ropes, fathers, a roof, and a ladder, ending with rosemary and hell.
counterfactuals.output:
We buried the evidence behind the house,  
where the yard stayed wet even in drought—  
a button, a tooth, a ribbon of blood  
hardened black in its paper envelope.

By morning it had sprouted.

First came beams, pale and knuckled,  
pushing through the soil like bones  
that had remembered the names of trees.  
Then rafters branched from them,  
creaking in the moonlight,  
a skeleton of shelter assembling itself  
over the guilty grass.

Ropes followed, flowering downward,  
braided from hair, hemp, and whispers.  
They swung without wind.  
They knew the weight of every throat  
in the village.

By the third night, fathers grew there—  
not men exactly, but father-shaped weather:  
boots full of rain, hands like locked doors,  
faces blurred as if seen through smoke.  
They stood beneath the rafters  
and called us home  
in voices borrowed from the dead.

Then the roof came in,  
shingled with old alibis,  
nailed down by crows.  
It covered the yard, the well, the window,  
the place where the dog refused to dig.  
Under it, daylight turned brown  
and the house began to breathe.

Last came the ladder,  
rising from the grave-soil plank by plank,  
each rung slick with testimony.  
It leaned against nothing  
and still invited us upward.

We climbed because the dead were watching.  
We climbed because the fathers pointed.  
At the top, there was no heaven—  
only a garden box, split open,  
rooted with rosemary and hell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
